deposit-vs-no-show-fee.html.text:
APPOINTMENT DEPOSIT CALCULATOR

Deposit or no-show fee — which should I charge?

Both exist to protect a slot on your calendar, but they act at different moments. A deposit is collected when the appointment is booked, before you know how it will go. A no-show fee is only charged afterward, and only if the appointment is missed. Confusing the two leads to the wrong policy — and sometimes to advertising a "no-show fee" that customers never actually see, because nothing was collected up front to enforce it against.

Side by side

DepositNo-show fee
CollectedAt booking, before the appointmentAfter a missed appointment, if at all
Applies toThe service price (reduces the balance due)Nothing — it is a separate charge for the missed slot
ReliabilityEasier: customer is motivated to secure the slotHarder: charged after the fact, often disputed
Effect on bookingsCan turn away price-sensitive prospects before they bookNo effect on booking volume; only affects no-shows
What it costs youThe bookings it turns away — which is the whole cost, so break-even is a booking rate, not a fee sizeNothing in bookings; the cost is the share you never manage to collect
This portfolio's toolThis calculatorNo-Show & Cancellation Fee Calculator

What the numbers look like

On this calculator's defaults — a $150 service, a 25% deposit — the deposit is $37.50, applied to the price, leaving a $112.50 balance due at the appointment. That $37.50 is in hand whether or not the customer eventually shows. At 12 bookings a week and an assumed 93% booking rate once the deposit is required, that is 11.16 bookings a week and $21,762 a year in deposits collected.

That $21,762 is not extra money, and it is the number most easily misread on this page. A deposit is applied to the service total rather than added to it, so the deposits collected in a year are revenue that would have been billed anyway, taken earlier. The question of whether a deposit leaves you better off is a different sum, and the calculator now does it: on the same defaults, plus a 15% no-show rate today and 5% once a deposit is required, a year comes to $79,560 with no deposit against $83,783.70 with one — $4,223.70 better, with break-even at an 88.3% booking rate. Keep more than 88.3% of today's bookings and the deposit is ahead; keep less and it is behind.

A no-show fee has no equivalent up-front number, because nothing is collected until a slot is actually missed. Its size is usually set as a share of the service price — the sibling calculator defaults to 100% of a $75 service, so $75 — but whether it is ever paid depends on being able to charge a card on file after the fact, and on local rules about that.

The two tools answer the two halves and neither repeats the other. This calculator asks whether requiring a deposit is worth what it costs you in bookings. The No-Show & Cancellation Fee Calculator takes the no-shows as given and asks how much of that lost revenue each policy claws back — a fee charged afterward, a forfeited deposit, or a deposit plus the remainder — at an enforcement rate you set for how often an after-the-fact charge actually gets paid. If you are choosing whether to have a deposit at all, start here; if you have decided and want to know which recovery policy collects most, start there.

Open the deposit calculator to model your own price, booking volume, expected booking rate, and no-show rates.

What this is not

  • Not advice on which policy to run, or that you must run either one.
  • Not a legal reading of what fees or deposits your jurisdiction or payment processor allow — check both before publishing a policy.
  • Not a claim that a deposit prevents no-shows; it changes who books, and the calculator's booking-rate input is your own estimate of that effect, not a guarantee.

Common questions

Should I charge a deposit or a no-show fee?

They answer different questions. A deposit is collected at booking, before you know whether the customer will show — on this calculator's defaults, $150 at 25% is a $37.50 deposit applied to the price, leaving a $112.50 balance due at the appointment. A no-show fee is only charged after the appointment is missed, and only exists as a policy you enforce afterward. A deposit secures cash and commitment up front; a no-show fee compensates you after the fact for a slot that already went empty.

Can I use both a deposit and a no-show fee?

Yes, and many service businesses do: the deposit is applied to the final price if the customer shows, and forfeited (acting as the no-show fee) if they cancel late or do not show. That is what this calculator's policy draft describes under its cancellation-notice window. A separate, larger no-show fee on top of a forfeited deposit is unusual and should be disclosed clearly before booking.

Which one actually gets paid?

A deposit is easier to collect, because it is taken while the customer is still booking and motivated to secure the slot. A no-show fee is charged after the fact, often against a saved card, and is harder to collect and more likely to be disputed. If cash-in-hand before the appointment matters more than punishing a no-show after it, a deposit is the more reliable mechanism.

Does a deposit stop no-shows?

It changes who books, not just who shows. On this calculator's defaults, requiring a 25% deposit is modeled as keeping 93% of the 12 weekly bookings you'd otherwise get — 11.16 a week — and collecting $21,762 a year in deposits at that rate. Those deposits are not profit: they are revenue you would have billed anyway, collected earlier. What the deposit is actually worth is the difference it makes to the year, which on those defaults plus a 15%-to-5% no-show improvement is $4,223.70, with break-even at an 88.3% booking rate. Some prospective customers who would have booked without a deposit will not book with one; the calculator asks you to estimate that trade-off rather than assuming it away.

Set an appointment deposit you can explain.

For salons, trainers, tutors, photographers, and other small service businesses. Common questions

What percentage should I charge?

Twenty to thirty percent is a useful starting range for many services, but the right amount depends on the price, preparation time, and how difficult the slot is to refill. This calculator shows your assumption; it does not decide for you. See the deposit, balance, and secured-cash numbers at five common percentages on a $150 service.

Does a deposit actually make me more money?

That is what the "Does the deposit pay for itself?" panel answers, and it is not the same question as how much cash a deposit secures. A deposit is applied to the service total rather than added to it, so the deposits you collect are revenue you would have billed anyway, collected earlier — not new money. The gain, if there is one, comes from appointments that are kept instead of missed, plus deposits forfeited by the no-shows that remain. The cost is the bookings you never get because a deposit was asked for. The calculator puts a year of each side next to the other using the no-show rates and booking rate you enter, and shows the difference.

What is the break-even booking rate?

It is the share of today's bookings you would have to keep for a deposit policy to match what you earn now. Keep more than that and the deposit is ahead on these assumptions; keep less and it is behind. It is usually below 100%, and the reason is the most useful thing this panel shows: as long as a deposit does not make no-shows worse, it pays for itself at full retention even if nobody's behaviour changes, because the no-shows that remain forfeit a deposit instead of paying nothing. The entire cost of a deposit policy is the bookings it turns away. A break-even above 100% only appears if you enter a higher no-show rate with a deposit than without one. The comparison assumes a missed appointment earns nothing and the slot is not refilled; if you reliably refill short-notice cancellations, a deposit is worth less to you than this shows.

Is a deposit a cancellation fee?

No. A deposit is an upfront payment applied to the service total. Your refund and cancellation terms should be disclosed before booking and checked against local rules and payment-provider requirements.

How is the deposit amount calculated?

Deposit equals your service price times the deposit percentage you enter, divided by 100. The balance due at the appointment is simply the service price minus that deposit — there is no separate processing fee or markup added by this tool.

Why does the calculator ask for a booking rate?

Requiring a deposit can turn away some prospective customers who would have booked without one, so the calculator asks what share of your usual weekly bookings you expect to keep once a deposit is required. It multiplies that rate against your weekly bookings, then by the deposit, then by 52 weeks, to model the cash a deposit policy secures over a year — not just the deposit on a single booking.

What happens if a customer cancels?

The policy this tool drafts treats the free-cancellation notice window you set as the cutoff: cancellations made at least that many hours before the appointment may be refunded or transferred, while cancellations with less notice, or no-shows, may forfeit the deposit. The exact terms are yours to set and should be checked against your local rules and payment provider's requirements before you publish them.

Does this tool recommend a deposit percentage for me?

No. It is deterministic math with no built-in advice or recommended percent — it turns the price and percentage you choose into a deposit amount, balance due, and secured-cash estimate, and drafts policy wording from your inputs. The percentage decision stays yours.

FOR TATTOO ARTISTS AND SHOPS

Deposit and touch-up pricing, in one place.

A tattoo deposit works the same way any service deposit does. What's different is the touch-up: most shops offer a free window after the original session, then charge for touch-ups after that. This calculator handles both — set the deposit, then check a specific client's touch-up against your free window and price it by percent, flat fee, or hourly rate if the window has closed.

Common questions

How much deposit should a tattoo shop charge?

There is no single correct amount — shops commonly ask for a flat amount or a percentage of the estimated session price, often in the 20-50% range for custom work. This calculator turns whatever percentage you choose into a dollar deposit and the balance still due; it does not tell you what percentage to charge.

Is a tattoo touch-up free?

That depends entirely on the shop's own policy, which this tool does not set for you. Many shops offer touch-ups free within a stated window after the original session (commonly a few months to a year) and charge for touch-ups requested after that window closes. Enter your own free-window length and how long ago the original session was, and the calculator reports which side of that window a specific client falls on.

How should a tattoo shop price a touch-up once it is no longer free?

Three common approaches: a percentage of the original session price, a flat fee regardless of the original price, or the shop's hourly rate multiplied by the estimated touch-up time. vs-doing-it-by-hand.html.text:
← Appointment deposit calculator

This calculator vs. doing it by hand or in a spreadsheet

Deposit and balance are one line of arithmetic—price times percentage, and whatever's left. Anyone can do that by hand or in a spreadsheet. The part that's easy to get wrong, or to skip entirely, is whether requiring a deposit actually leaves you with more money once you account for the customers a deposit turns away and the no-shows it prevents. That's the step this calculator was built for.

What each approach actually does

By hand or in a spreadsheet, you can compute the deposit amount, the balance due, and even a rough sense of how much cash a year of deposits secures. All of that is straightforward multiplication and subtraction, and a correctly built spreadsheet gets it exactly right. What a spreadsheet does not give you, unless you build it in yourself, is a prompt to check whether the deposit is actually worth charging — because “cash secured” on its own looks like a gain even though it is mostly revenue you would have billed anyway, just collected earlier.

This calculator takes the same inputs — service price, deposit percentage, bookings per week, an expected booking rate once a deposit is required, and no-show rates with and without one — and adds the comparison a spreadsheet does not set up on its own: yearly revenue with the deposit against yearly revenue without it, the difference, and the break-even booking rate at which the policy stops paying for itself. It then turns the same inputs into a policy paragraph you can paste into whichever booking system you already use.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What is the deposit amount and the balance due?Either — price × percentage, and the remainder. A spreadsheet gets this exactly right too.
How much cash does a year of deposits secure?Either can multiply it out, but see the next row before reading that figure as profit.
Does requiring a deposit actually leave me with more money once fewer people book and fewer no-show?This calculator's “Does the deposit pay for itself?” panel — a spreadsheet has to be built to ask this, and most aren't.
What booking rate would I need to keep for the deposit to break even?This calculator solves for it directly. By hand, it's a formula you'd have to set up and re-check every time an input changes.
I want a policy paragraph to actually publish.This calculator drafts one from your numbers. A spreadsheet doesn't write prose.
My situation has a wrinkle this calculator doesn't model (a partial refund tier, a sliding deposit scale).A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can represent any rule you can describe.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No, either way — a local spreadsheet and this calculator both keep your numbers on your own device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Can't I just work out the deposit and balance by hand?

Yes — deposit is service price times deposit percentage, and balance is whatever is left. That part is one line of arithmetic and a spreadsheet does it exactly as well as this calculator does. Where a hand calculation or a quick spreadsheet formula stops short is the harder question underneath it: given your own no-show rates and how a deposit changes how many people actually book, does requiring one leave you with more money at the end of the year, or less. That comparison has more moving parts than deposit-times-percentage, and it is the part this calculator exists for.

What does a spreadsheet not check that this calculator does?

Whether the deposit pays for itself. A spreadsheet will happily multiply your weekly bookings by the deposit and call the result "revenue secured" — but that figure is money you would have billed anyway, collected earlier, not new income, and reading it as a gain is the mistake this calculator's own FAQ warns against. The real trade has a cost side too: some prospective customers do not book at all once a deposit is required. A spreadsheet built from scratch has no built-in prompt to model that cost against the benefit of fewer no-shows; this calculator puts both sides of the trade next to each other and shows the break-even booking rate — the share of today's bookings you would need to keep for the policy to be worth it at all.

Is the break-even booking rate something I could work out myself?

With the right formula, yes — it is the booking rate at which yearly revenue with the deposit equals yearly revenue without one, given both no-show rates and the deposit amount. Setting that formula up correctly, and re-deriving it correctly every time a price or a no-show estimate changes, is exactly the kind of one-time-easy, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong-later math this calculator exists to remove. A copied cell reference or a forgotten weighting is not obvious in the output the way a typo in a deposit percentage is.

Does a spreadsheet draft the policy wording too?

Not unless you write it yourself. Once the numbers are decided, the policy still has to say, in plain language, what the deposit is, what the balance is, and what happens if the customer cancels with or without notice — and it has to do that in a way clients actually read. This calculator turns your inputs straight into a policy paragraph you can paste into whichever booking system you already use; a spreadsheet, however good its formulas, still leaves that paragraph for you to draft separately.

Is this calculator affiliated with any spreadsheet software?

There is nothing to be affiliated with. This page compares against doing the arithmetic by hand or building your own spreadsheet — a generic method, not any specific company or product — so it names no spreadsheet application, booking platform, or vendor at all.

This calculator vs. Square Appointments

Two different jobs: Square Appointments is an account-based booking and payments platform for running a service business's whole diary. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should the deposit be, and does charging it actually leave you with more money — before that number goes into any booking system's settings.

What each tool is for

Square Appointments is a booking and point-of-sale platform from Block, Inc. (formerly Square, Inc.), founded in 2009 by Jack Dorsey and Jim McKelvey and headquartered in San Francisco. It gives clients a booking page to schedule themselves, syncs calendars and staff schedules, sends automated reminders, and, through Square's own payment processing, can require a card on file or a deposit before a booking is confirmed. It is built for salons, spas, trainers, tutors, photographers, and other service businesses to run their whole client-facing diary and take payment through one account. Square's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's plan names or processing rates, so no dollar figure for Square Appointments is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — an account-based booking and payments platform with deposit and no-show protection features — are stated.

This calculator does none of what Square Appointments does. It has no booking page, no calendar, no client list, and no connection to a payment processor — it stores and charges nothing. It takes one service price, a deposit percentage, bookings per week, an expected booking rate once a deposit is required, and no-show rates with and without a deposit, and turns them into the deposit amount, the balance due at the appointment, the cash a year of deposits secures, a side-by-side of yearly revenue with and without the deposit so you can see whether it actually pays for itself, and a policy paragraph you can paste into whichever booking system you already use. what-percentage-deposit-should-i-charge..text:
← Appointment deposit calculator

What percentage deposit should you charge? Here is the arithmetic at five common rates.

Every service business asks this before setting a policy. There is no universally correct percentage — the ones businesses actually charge range from about 15% up to 40% or more for high-cost or high-no-show services. What changes, predictably, is the dollar deposit, the balance still due, and how much cash a year of bookings secures. See the numbers first, then decide.

Five deposit percentages on a $150 service

Same $150 service price and the calculator's default 12 bookings/week at a 93% booking rate. Arithmetic only — no recommendation.
Deposit % Deposit due at booking Balance due at service Secured cash per year*
15%$22.50$127.50$13,057.20
20%$30.00$120.00$17,409.60
25%$37.50$112.50$21,762.00
30%$45.00$105.00$26,114.40
40%$60.00$90.00$34,819.20

*At an unchanged 11.16 completed bookings a week (12 weekly bookings × 93% booking rate × 52 weeks). The calculator does not lower this rate automatically as the percentage rises — that assumption is yours to set, because only you can estimate how a bigger deposit changes who actually books.

Deposit and balance move in lockstep with the percentage: deposit is simply price × percent, and balance is whatever is left of the price. The number that is easy to miss is the last column — the spread between a 15% and a 40% deposit on secured cash is $21,762 a year on this one example, before any change in how many people book at all.

Two things push most small service businesses toward the low end of that range: a lower deposit is a smaller ask of someone who has not experienced the service yet, and it reads as less risky to a first-time customer deciding whether to commit. Two things push toward the high end: a service with expensive material or prep cost that is wasted on a no-show, and a customer base that already trusts the business enough that the percentage rarely changes their decision to book.

Open the calculator, put in your own service price, bookings per week, and booking-rate assumption, and read your own deposit, balance, and secured-cash figures before you write a policy. Nothing you enter is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not legal, tax, or financial advice. It does not tell you what percentage to charge or claim a policy is compliant with your local rules or payment provider's terms.

Common questions

What percentage deposit should I charge for an appointment?

There is no single correct percentage — 15% to 40% are all common in practice. The trade-off is mechanical: a higher percentage secures more cash per booking and covers more of your cost if someone no-shows, but it is also more money a new customer has to commit before they have used your service, which can lower how many people complete the booking. Pick a starting percentage, watch your actual completion rate for a few weeks, and adjust.

Does a higher deposit percentage always secure more money over a year?

Only if your booking rate stays the same, and this calculator does not assume that for you. Raising the percentage from 25% to 40% on a $150 service raises the deposit from $37.50 to $60, which — at an unchanged 93% booking rate on 12 weekly bookings — raises secured cash from $21,762 to $34,819.20 a year.
